questions.topic: Inner Joins: Matching Rows on Keys
questions.question: Which mental model correctly captures what `FROM a JOIN b ON cond` means?
options: Merge the two tables column-wise, then remove any rows containing NULLs
Form all pairs of rows from both tables, then keep pairs where the condition is TRUE
Look up each row of `a` in an index on `b`, then discard rows lacking index entries
Append the rows of `b` beneath the rows of `a`, then filter on the condition

questions.topic: Inner Joins: Matching Rows on Keys
questions.question: Two tables are joined with `ON a.k = b.k`, and both tables contain rows where `k` is NULL. How do those rows behave?
options: They match each other, since both sides hold the same NULL marker
They match every row, since NULL comparisons default to TRUE in ON
They raise an error, since join key columns must be declared NOT NULL
They match nothing, since `NULL = NULL` is UNKNOWN and only TRUE joins

questions.topic: Inner Joins: Matching Rows on Keys
questions.question: `users` has 3 rows (ids 1, 2, 3). `orders` has 3 rows with user_id values 1, 1, 3. What does an inner join on user_id return?
options: Three rows, with user 2 absent because it has no matching order
Two rows, with user 1 collapsed to one row despite two matching orders
Four rows, with user 2 kept once and padded with NULL order columns
Nine rows, with every user paired against every order in the table

questions.topic: Inner Joins: Matching Rows on Keys
questions.question: For an inner join, a filter like `o.amount > 100` can go in ON or in WHERE. What is the practical difference?
options: ON applies the filter before the join, so it returns more rows than WHERE
WHERE applies the filter per table, so it runs faster than the ON version
The results are identical; keeping keys in ON is purely a readability habit
The results differ whenever the filtered column contains any NULL values

questions.topic: Inner Joins: Matching Rows on Keys
questions.question: Before writing a join, an experienced engineer first settles which question?
options: What does one row represent on each side, and is the join key unique there?
Which of the two tables involved will hold more rows at execution time?
Does the engine plan a hash join or a nested loop for this predicate?
Are the two join columns declared with exactly the same data type?

questions.topic: Inner Joins: Matching Rows on Keys
questions.question: A query joins events to campaigns with `ON e.created_at BETWEEN c.start_at AND c.end_at`. A reviewer objects that joins must compare keys for equality. Who is right?
options: The reviewer, because non-equality conditions are only legal in WHERE
The reviewer, because range predicates make join results nondeterministic
The author, because the engine rewrites range joins into key equality anyway
The author, because ON accepts any predicate and range joins are legitimate

questions.topic: LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL Outer Joins and Unmatched Rows
questions.question: What does a LEFT JOIN guarantee that an inner join does not?
options: Every matched pair appears exactly once, with duplicate rows removed
Every row of the right table appears, padded with NULLs when unmatched
Every row of the left table appears, padded with NULLs when unmatched
Every row of both tables appears, matched or padded as necessary

questions.topic: LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL Outer Joins and Unmatched Rows
questions.question: Which task is the canonical use of a FULL OUTER JOIN?
options: Attaching parent attributes to every child row in a one-to-many pair
Reconciling two dataset versions to surface adds and deletes on a key
Removing the duplicate rows produced when a join key is not unique
Checking that a foreign key has a matching row for every reference

questions.topic: LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL Outer Joins and Unmatched Rows
questions.question: A LEFT JOIN from users to orders is followed by `WHERE o.amount > 100`, and users without orders vanish from the result. Why?
options: The engine promotes any filtered LEFT JOIN to a FULL JOIN, dropping padding
WHERE runs before the join, so unmatched users never get produced at all
LEFT JOIN padding survives only when the query has no WHERE clause at all
Padded rows have NULL amount, the predicate is UNKNOWN, and WHERE drops them

questions.topic: LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL Outer Joins and Unmatched Rows
questions.question: You want every user in the result, joined only to their orders above 100. Which query expresses that?
options: `LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.user_id AND o.amount > 100`
`LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.user_id WHERE o.amount > 100`
`JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.user_id AND o.amount > 100`
`JOIN orders o ON o.user_id = u.user_id WHERE o.amount >= 100`

questions.topic: LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL Outer Joins and Unmatched Rows
questions.question: After `users LEFT JOIN orders`, you filter `WHERE o.notes IS NULL` to find users without orders, where `notes` is an optional text column. What is wrong?
options: Nothing is wrong, since any right-side column is NULL exactly when unmatched
Matched orders with empty notes also pass, so test a NOT NULL column like the PK
IS NULL cannot follow an outer join, so the filter must move into the ON clause
The filter must test the left side's key, since the right side is never NULL

questions.topic: LEFT, RIGHT, and FULL Outer Joins and Unmatched Rows
questions.question: Why do experienced SQL authors rarely write RIGHT JOIN?
options: Because most engines have deprecated it in favor of FULL OUTER JOIN
Because RIGHT JOIN cannot preserve unmatched rows from either table
Because swapping the tables expresses it as a LEFT JOIN that reads better
Because RIGHT JOIN forces the optimizer into a slower execution strategy

questions.topic: Semi-Joins and Anti-Joins with EXISTS and NOT EXISTS
questions.question: What distinguishes a semi-join via EXISTS from an ordinary inner join?
options: It returns columns from both tables but limits output to matched pairs
It returns rows only when exactly one matching row exists on the far side
It returns the matching rows of the inner table instead of the outer one
It returns each outer row at most once, however many rows match it

questions.topic: Semi-Joins and Anti-Joins with EXISTS and NOT EXISTS
questions.question: In `WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.user_id = u.user_id)`, what does the `SELECT 1` contribute?
options: Nothing of substance; EXISTS only checks whether any row comes back
A flag column whose value EXISTS compares against the constant TRUE
A limit instructing the probe to stop after scanning exactly one page
A count that EXISTS tests for being greater than or equal to one

questions.topic: Semi-Joins and Anti-Joins with EXISTS and NOT EXISTS
questions.question: `WHERE u.user_id NOT IN (SELECT user_id FROM orders)` starts returning zero rows after a data change, while the NOT EXISTS version still works. What changed?
options: orders grew past the size limit that IN-list expansion can handle
A duplicate user_id appeared, which NOT IN treats as a contradiction
A NULL user_id appeared in orders, making every NOT IN test UNKNOWN
An index on orders.user_id was dropped, which NOT IN requires to run

questions.topic: Semi-Joins and Anti-Joins with EXISTS and NOT EXISTS
questions.question: A query joins users to orders just to list users who ordered, then applies DISTINCT to remove duplicates. What is the better formulation, and why?
options: Keep the join but add LIMIT, because truncation removes duplicated users
Use EXISTS, because a semi-join never multiplies rows and stops at the first hit
Use a FULL JOIN, because unmatched padding makes duplicates easy to filter
Keep DISTINCT but move it inside ON, because deduplication belongs to joins

questions.topic: Semi-Joins and Anti-Joins with EXISTS and NOT EXISTS
questions.question: How does `NOT EXISTS` compare to the LEFT JOIN plus `IS NULL` idiom for finding unmatched rows?
options: NOT EXISTS returns extra rows whenever the probe table has duplicate keys
LEFT JOIN plus IS NULL is faster because it avoids probing per outer row
They differ on NULL keys, where the LEFT JOIN version silently drops rows
They express the same anti-join, and optimizers usually run both alike

questions.topic: Semi-Joins and Anti-Joins with EXISTS and NOT EXISTS
questions.question: During review you see a DISTINCT that was added because a count 'came out too high'. What should this signal?
options: The table statistics are stale and the optimizer needs a manual refresh
The query's grain likely broke upstream, and the duplication needs a root cause
The join columns have mismatched types that force redundant comparisons
The engine chose a hash join where only a nested loop keeps rows unique

questions.topic: Join Fan-out: Row Duplication When Keys Are Not Unique
questions.question: A join key value appears 3 times in the left table and 4 times in the right table. How many rows does the join emit for that value?
options: 12, one for every pairing of left and right rows sharing the value
7, one for each row on either side that carries the shared value
4, one for each right row, with the left rows collapsed into one
3, one for each left row, keeping the left table's original grain

questions.topic: Join Fan-out: Row Duplication When Keys Are Not Unique
questions.question: Which join shape is guaranteed not to multiply the left table's rows?
options: A join where the left table's key column contains no NULL values
A join between two tables that each hold fewer than a million rows
A join whose key is unique on the right side, as in FK to PK lookups
A join written with explicit JOIN syntax rather than comma-separated FROM

questions.topic: Join Fan-out: Row Duplication When Keys Are Not Unique
questions.question: A revenue report joins users to orders and to logins in one query, then totals order amounts. Revenue is overstated by a different factor per user. Which defect explains it?
options: The orders table double-counts refunds, inflating users with returns most
The join dropped users without logins, skewing the denominator per user
NULL amounts were coalesced to averages, drifting each user differently
Each order was duplicated once per login row, so users differ by login count

questions.topic: Join Fan-out: Row Duplication When Keys Are Not Unique
questions.question: You need per-user order totals and per-user login counts in one result. What is the fan-out-safe approach?
options: Reduce each side to one row per user first, then join the two summaries
Join all three tables first, then divide each total by the login count
Join orders to logins directly so the duplication cancels symmetrically
Use a FULL JOIN so unmatched rows offset the duplicated matched rows

questions.topic: Join Fan-out: Row Duplication When Keys Are Not Unique
questions.question: A pipeline query is supposed to return exactly one row per user. Which safeguard most directly catches a future fan-out regression?
options: A code comment documenting that every join in the query is one-to-one
A post-query assertion that the result's row count equals the user count
A DISTINCT on user_id so duplicated rows collapse before downstream use
A LIMIT set to the user count so extra duplicated rows get truncated

questions.topic: Join Fan-out: Row Duplication When Keys Are Not Unique
questions.question: When reading an unfamiliar multi-join query, what question does an experienced reviewer ask of each individual join?
options: Which index will the optimizer pick to execute this join efficiently?
Should this join move into the WHERE clause for earlier filtering?
What can this join multiply, given key uniqueness on each side?
Would this join return the same rows if written as a RIGHT JOIN?
